title: Public homepage
summary: The homepage looks calm and well made, and the headline says what Eleva is in one line, but it never shows a member a single expert they can book: the only named faces are advisors, and the route to a real expert is one generic button. Proof is thin (four two-word labels, no member voice, no numbers) and the page ends on a pitch to experts. The change that matters most is to put the choice of need and a row of real, bookable experts in the first two screens, and move the advisors below them as supporting proof.
strengths: The headline 'Women's health experts, on your schedule.' plus the lead line answers what Eleva is and who it is for in under ten seconds. Keep both.
Lora headings on cream with deep teal read as calm and premium, not clinical. The type scale and spacing are consistent from section to section.
The board of advisors is real proof: named people with credentials and a quote. Few health marketplaces at this stage have that.
'No waiting lists and no account needed to book' is a strong, concrete promise, and the three steps are written in plain words.
One label, 'Find an expert', is used in the header, the hero and on mobile, so the main action is never renamed.
The 'Grow your practice with Eleva' band is clearly for a different audience: its own block, its own coral button, at the end of the page.

findings.title: No bookable expert appears anywhere on the homepage
findings.detail: The page shows eight advisors by name and face, and zero experts a member can book. A first-time visitor reads the advisor portraits as 'these are the experts', then the lead tells her 'Your care comes from the independent expert you choose', and the page never shows who that could be. Reaching one real person takes Find an expert, then the directory, then a profile. For a marketplace the supply is the product; hiding it makes the page feel like a brochure and is the main reason it reads as weak.
findings.recommendation: Add a 'Meet our experts' row directly under the value strip: four to six real expert cards with photo, name, profession, languages, how they meet (video, phone, in person), price from, and the next free slot, each linking to the profile, plus 'See all experts'. On a phone make it a horizontal scroll so a card and a half is visible. Design the card for a new expert with no photo and a short bio (initials on a brand tint, profession and languages still carry the card). Rotate by category so every profession gets shown.

findings.title: The hero offers one generic button and no way to start from a need
findings.detail: A member arrives with a need (pelvic pain after birth, breastfeeding, menopause), but the hero gives her only 'Find an expert'. The category chips sit two screens down on desktop and about four screens down on a phone, after three full-width advisor portraits. The two photo cards beside the hero ('Care for every stage of life', 'Experts who listen') look like navigation but are captions that link to /experts/wellness and /experts, and they disappear on mobile.
findings.recommendation: Let the member say what she needs inside the hero. Either a single search field ('What do you need help with?') with the nine categories as suggestions, or a row of five or six need chips under the lead line that go straight to the filtered directory. Replace the two caption cards with need tiles that name a real destination (Pregnancy and postpartum, Pelvic health, Menopause). Keep 'Find an expert' as the fallback button.

findings.title: Proof is four short labels; no member voice, no numbers, no word on how experts are checked
findings.detail: The strip under the hero reads 'Independent experts', 'Online or in person', 'In your language', 'Clear prices'. Each is a claim with nothing behind it, set in small text with wide gaps, so it is easy to miss. The page has no member story, no count of experts or professions, and it never says that Eleva checks each expert's professional registration, which the become-expert page does say. A woman deciding whether to pay a stranger for health care needs exactly that sentence.
findings.recommendation: Turn the strip into four claims with substance, for example 'Every expert's professional registration is checked before they go live', 'Video, phone or in person', 'Sessions in English, Portuguese and Spanish', 'You see the price before you book'. Add a short 'Who you will meet' block with honest figures (experts live, professions covered, advisors on the board) and link it to the trust page. When members consent, add two or three short stories tagged by need. Use real numbers only; a small true number beats none.

findings.title: Advisors come before the offer and are told twice
findings.detail: The board of advisors is the first section after the hero, ahead of the services, and the same authority returns four sections later as a full-width teal quote from Kari Bø. On a phone the three advisor portraits stack at full width (roughly 1,200px of scrolling) before a member sees what she can book. The advisors are strong proof, but in this position they delay the offer and blur who delivers the care.
findings.recommendation: Merge the two sections into one compact band placed after the experts and services: the lead advisor's quote with her portrait, a row of the other seven faces with name and one-line credential, the universities or institutions they come from as a logo line, and 'Meet the board'. On mobile show the quote plus a single row of small faces, not three full-width portraits.

findings.title: Two competing ways to browse: nine profession chips and four life-stage photo cards
findings.detail: 'Expert-led care, tailored to you' shows nine chips named by profession (Psychology, Midwifery, Lactation...) and under them four stock-photo cards named by life stage (Pregnancy and postpartum, Pelvic health, Through every stage...). They are two taxonomies for the same directory, and neither says what a member will find behind it. The photo cards are the part of the page that looks most like a template, and on a phone they add four tall cards in a column.
findings.recommendation: Use one grid, 'Start from what you need', with six to eight tiles. Each tile names the need in the member's words, lists two or three example services ('Pelvic floor assessment', 'Return to exercise after birth') and shows how many experts offer it. Keep professions as a filter inside the directory. On mobile lay the tiles out two per row, or as one scrolling row.

findings.title: 'How it works' explains the product without showing it
findings.detail: Three numbered text rows sit beside one stock photo of a woman at a laptop. Nothing shows what booking on Eleva looks like, so the section could belong to any service. The strongest line on the page, 'No waiting lists and no account needed to book', is set as grey lead text.
findings.recommendation: Give each step a small piece of the real interface: an expert card for 'Find your expert', the date and time picker for 'Book a time', the confirmation email with its Join button for 'Meet your expert'. Promote 'No account needed to book' into the hero or the value strip, and end the section with a 'Find an expert' button.

findings.title: The space under the hero headline is spent on a slogan, a hedge and the other audience
findings.detail: The eyebrow 'Women's health, elevated' is a slogan that adds no information. The second hero button is 'Become an expert', which gives the most valuable spot on the page to a different audience that already has a nav menu and its own band. The line under the buttons, 'Eleva connects you with independent health experts who run their own practice', reads as a legal hedge where a reassurance should be.
findings.recommendation: Drop the eyebrow or use it for place and language ('Portugal · English, Portuguese, Spanish'). Replace the second button with 'How it works' or with need chips (see HOME-02) and leave expert recruitment to the header and the band. Rewrite the last line as a benefit that still states the model: 'You choose your expert. They run their own practice; Eleva takes care of booking and payment.'

findings.title: On a phone the page is about 27 screens long and the first screen is only the hero
findings.detail: The mobile capture is 10,566px tall. The hero fills the whole first screen with a dimmed video in which a face sits directly behind the headline, the header carries four unlabelled icons (globe, person, search, menu), and the value strip wraps into an uneven two-by-two block. Advisors, service cards and the how-it-works photo each stack at full width, and the footer alone is about 1,900px.
findings.recommendation: Shorten the mobile hero so the value strip and the top of the next section show on the first screen, and use a still crop that keeps faces clear of the text. Make the strip a tidy two-column grid. Turn advisors, experts and need tiles into horizontal rows. Target under 6,500px in total. Label or reduce the header icons: logo, 'Find an expert', menu.

findings.title: The page ends on the pitch to experts, with no questions answered and no closing action for members
findings.detail: The last three blocks are a belief statement ('Women's health is a lifelong journey'), a link to the mission, and 'Grow your practice with Eleva'. A member who has scrolled the whole page still has open questions (what a session costs, how a video session works, whether she can cancel, who the experts are) and the final button she sees is 'Become an expert'.
findings.recommendation: Add a short FAQ before the expert band with five or six questions in the member's words: What is Eleva? Who are the experts and how are they checked? How much does a session cost? How do online sessions work? Can I cancel or reschedule? Do I need an account? Close with a member call to action ('Find an expert') and keep the expert band as the last, clearly separate block. Fold the belief statement into the About page or into one line above the FAQ.

findings.title: The footer is dominated by fourteen legal links and has no way back into care
findings.detail: The Legal column lists fourteen links and is twice the height of the others. The first column is titled 'Join Eleva' but holds About and Our story. There is no 'Find care' column with the categories, no contact or help line, and no language switch. On a phone the footer is a single list about 1,900px long.
findings.recommendation: Regroup into Find care (the categories), For professionals, Company, and Help. Keep four or five legal links visible (Terms, Privacy, Health data, Cookies, Complaints book) and put the rest behind 'All policies'. Add the Femme Focus newsletter sign-up and the language switch. On mobile collapse the columns into accordions.

findings.title: Sections start invisible until scrolled, and the hero loads empty
findings.detail: The large empty areas in the two JPEGs (under 'Guided by leaders', under the category chips, the dark teal band, beside the steps and beside 'Our belief') are not empty on the live page. Those blocks use a scroll-driven fade from zero opacity, which a full-page screenshot never triggers; the scroll videos show the advisor cards, care cards, quote and photos in place. The stills were re-captured with reduced motion on 2026-11-14 and now show the content. Two real points remain: the first video frame shows the hero panel and both side cards with no image while media loads, and any tool that renders the page without scrolling (previews, print, some screenshot services) gets the blank version. No Mobbin reference was found for this; it is an implementation point.
findings.recommendation: Give the hero video a poster image and the side cards a colour placeholder so the first paint is never an empty dark panel. Keep the entrance animation to a small upward move and start it from a visible state (for example 60% opacity) so no content is ever fully hidden.

findings.title: Ten unrelated stock photographs and one repeated section layout set the look
findings.detail: The page shows about ten stock photographs (the hero video, the two side cards, four care cards, the how-it-works photo, the belief photo and the expert band) and they do not match: street daylight, a pale studio, a saturated outdoor group shot, a gym wall. None shows an Eleva expert or the product. Five sections in a row use the same layout: a mono eyebrow, a two-line serif heading whose second half is italic, a grey lead and a row of rounded images. Each part is well made, but the repetition and the mixed photographs are what make the page read as a template. On a phone the same photos stack at full width and account for much of the 10,566px.
findings.recommendation: Choose one image treatment and hold it: one crop, one warm grade, and a cream or teal brand tile where there is no good photograph. Keep photographs for what is real (experts, advisors, the product) and cut the rest. Make two sections typographic only (the need grid, the numbers). Vary the composition from one section to the next: centred, two unequal columns, a full-width band, a ruled grid. Use the italic half-heading once per screen at most.

findings.title: The advisor quote reads as a treatment claim, in clinical words, at display size
findings.detail: The homepage sets one sentence in very large type on a deep band: 'Evidence-based pelvic-floor muscle training not only prevents and treats dysfunction; it empowers women to live confidently and fully at every stage of life.' Three blind judges of the brand lab (2026-11-23), each working alone, flagged it: it promises a result, it uses clinical words a member would not, and it is the loudest sentence on the page. Her role reads 'Board advisor', which is an internal title.
findings.recommendation: Replace the quote with a plain statement of what advisors do for Eleva ('Guided by people who study women's health', then one line), name her as 'Advisor to Eleva' with her institution, and keep any quote short, in her own plain words and approved by her. Counsel reads the final wording, because a health claim on a public page is theirs to judge.

references.pattern: Hero that is the search, with a live booking count
references.why: The hero is a headline, one search bar with four fields (treatment or venue, location, date, time) and a single line of proof, '217,913 appointments booked today'. There is nothing else to read before acting, and the business audience is a small 'For business' button in the header.
references.apply: Make the hero the start of the search: one 'What do you need help with?' field or need chips, and one line of true proof under it. Move 'Become an expert' out of the hero and into the header. Wellness booking marketplace, close to Eleva's model.
references.query: telehealth marketplace hero section with search

references.pattern: Need tiles inside the hero, with a proof line beneath
references.why: Directly under the headline sit five tiles, one per condition, each a photo, a name and an arrow. Beside the headline is one prompt, 'Tell us what we can help you with', and under the tiles a single strip carries proof ('Loved and trusted by over 1 million subscribers') next to service facts.
references.apply: Put Eleva's needs (pregnancy and postpartum, pelvic health, lactation, menopause, nutrition, mental health) in the first screen as tiles, and merge the chips and the four care cards into this one grid. Fill the strip under it with claims that carry proof.
references.query: telehealth marketplace hero section with search

references.pattern: Provider cards with rating and 'See availability' on the home screen (mobile)
references.why: On a phone-width screen the home shows a 'Search specialty' field, a short list of care types each with a Book button, then 'Providers nearby': a card with a round photo, name, specialty, distance, rating with review count and a 'See availability' button, with the next card peeking in from the right.
references.apply: The model for Eleva's 'Meet our experts' row on mobile: one and a half cards visible, the facts a member needs to choose, and a button that goes to times, not to a generic directory. iOS reference; the layout carries to mobile web.
references.query: therapist booking app home screen

references.pattern: Expert card grid with verified badge and availability status
references.why: Each card carries a 'Certified expert' label and badge, a photo or logo, a green 'Accepting new clients' status, the name, a three-line bio that truncates cleanly, and a star rating with count. Cards with a logo instead of a face, and one marked 'Not accepting new clients', sit in the same grid without breaking it.
references.apply: The card anatomy for Eleva's featured experts on desktop: a 'Registration checked' mark, a status line (next free slot), a bio capped at three lines, and a layout that still works with no photo. From a software experts directory; kept for its structure only.
references.query: expert booking marketplace featured experts section

references.pattern: 'Provider network' block: who delivers the care, with numbers
references.why: One block explains that care comes from 'rigorously vetted, independent, licensed practitioners', shows a cluster of their faces, and backs it with tiles: '800+ providers', '100% professionally licensed', a coverage figure, 'Rigorous qualifications', 'Ongoing customer support'.
references.apply: Eleva has the same model (independent experts, the platform is the technology) and currently states it as a disclaimer. Say it as a strength, with faces and honest figures: experts live, professions, '100% registration checked', languages.
references.query: therapy marketplace featured providers section

references.pattern: Advisor row with institution logos
references.why: A two-line heading, three institution logos (Stanford, Harvard Medical School, UCLA) at the right, and five equal portrait cards in one row, each with a name and a one-line credential. The whole board fits in one short band.
references.apply: Show all eight Eleva advisors in one compact row with name and a single credential line, and add the universities and institutions they belong to as a logo line. One band, placed after the experts and services.
references.query: health app medical advisors section

references.pattern: Lead advisor with a first-person quote, the rest of the board in a row below
references.why: The section names its lead advisor with title and institution, gives him a large portrait and a two-paragraph quote in his own words about why he joined, then lists four more advisors as a row of smaller portraits with name and role.
references.apply: Combine Eleva's advisor grid and the separate teal quote band into this one structure: Kari Bø's quote and portrait lead, the other seven sit in a row beneath. Ask for a quote about Eleva itself, in her words.
references.query: health app medical advisors section

references.pattern: Member stories tagged by need, one told in depth
references.why: A quoted headline in the member's words, a two-sentence summary and a 'Read Aimee's story' link sit beside a portrait video; two further quote cards are each tagged with the service used and titled by the health topic ('PCOS & IBS answers'). Cream, serif and a warm accent, close to Eleva's own palette.
references.apply: When members consent, add one story told in a few lines plus two short quotes, each tagged with the need (pelvic health, lactation) so a reader finds her own situation. Shows the pattern sits well in Eleva's visual language.
references.query: telehealth testimonials section

references.pattern: Three steps, each illustrated with a piece of the real interface
references.why: Three cards numbered 01 to 03, each with a short title, one line of text and a small interface fragment: a date and time picker, a results chart, a plan list. Two buttons close the section ('Start testing', 'See how it works').
references.apply: Replace the single stock photo with three interface fragments: an expert card, Eleva's slot picker, the confirmation email with the Join button. End the section with 'Find an expert'.
references.query: healthcare booking how it works section

references.pattern: FAQ that starts with 'What is it?' and 'Who are the providers?'
references.why: A plain accordion with large questions. The first, open by default, is 'What is Hims?', answered in two short paragraphs; the next are 'How does Hims work?' and 'Who are the providers at Hims?', followed by cost and coverage questions.
references.apply: Add a six-question FAQ near the end of the homepage in this order: what Eleva is, who the experts are and how they are checked, cost, how sessions work, cancelling, and whether an account is needed. First answer open.
references.query: telehealth FAQ section

references.pattern: Footer with three short columns, a newsletter sign-up and policies in one small row
references.why: Three link columns of six items each (Company, Explore, Community), a newsletter sign-up with a concrete offer, social icons, and the policy links reduced to one small row; the long legal text sits below the card in small print.
references.apply: Balance Eleva's footer the same way: short columns of similar length, the Femme Focus sign-up in the footer, and legal links cut to the essential few with the rest behind 'All policies'.
references.query: health company footer

references.pattern: A question as the headline, one search field and nine topic chips under it
references.why: The hero is a question ('how can we help you?'), one wide search field and nine chips that wrap onto a second row, all inside a cream band with a rounded lower edge. One chip is tinted to mark what is new. Nothing else competes, and the next section's heading already shows below the band.
references.apply: The layout for Eleva's hero: 'What do you need help with?' as the field and the nine areas of care as chips under it, aligned to the left edge of the field so two rows still look tidy. Nine chips fit without a carousel. Tint a chip only when there is a reason. From a note-taking app's help centre; kept for its structure only.
references.query: hero section with suggestion chips under a search field

references.pattern: Needs written as underlined text links under a serif statement, ending in 'Browse all'
references.why: A three-line serif statement says who the experts are ('hand-selected consultants and agencies'). Directly under it five needs sit as underlined text links in two short rows, followed by 'Browse all' with an arrow. There are no boxes or icons, so the type carries the block and it still reads as a list of choices. A video starts below and overlaps the edge of the band.
references.apply: A quieter option than chips for Eleva's hero or need section: five or six needs as underlined links in DM Sans under a Lora line, ending in 'See all areas'. It suits the serif and removes a row of pills from a page that already has many. From a software experts directory on a dark ground; kept for the composition only.
references.query: find a therapist website hero section

references.pattern: Three facts on the lower edge of the hero, inside the frame
references.why: The headline, one line of text and one button sit bottom left over a full-width photograph. Bottom right, on the same baseline, three facts are split by thin vertical rules, each a bold value over a short label ('Up to 30+ Assessments', 'Clinician-led Expert medical guidance'). The facts belong to the first screen and need no band of their own.
references.apply: Move Eleva's value claims onto the lower edge of the hero as value-over-label pairs ('Registration checked, every expert', 'Video, phone or in person', 'English, Portuguese, Spanish', 'Price shown before you book'), so they show on the first screen at every width. On a phone they become a two-by-two grid under the button. Keep faces in the photograph clear of the text column. Health membership product.
references.query: health service closing call to action section

references.pattern: A row of real people with the check stated in the row's heading
references.why: The heading does two jobs: it says what to do and that everyone shown was checked ('Browse background checked tutors near Menlo Park, CA'). Six square portraits of one size follow, each with a first name and initial, the place, a price from and years of experience, and some with a line of local proof ('Hired by 2 neighbors'). An arrow at the right shows the row continues. The photos are the people's own and uneven, and the fixed square crop still holds the row together.
references.apply: Eleva's 'Meet our experts' row on desktop: a heading that carries the trust claim ('Experts with a checked registration, ready to book'), five or six equal portrait tiles and three short lines under each (profession, languages, price from with the next time). The whole tile links to the profile. Care marketplace outside health; kept for the row and its heading.
references.query: coaching marketplace browse coaches page with specialty filter

references.pattern: Expert portraits on flat brand colours, with the name set on the image
references.why: A centred two-line heading, one sentence and one button sit above a row of tall portrait cards that runs off both edges of the screen. Each person is shown from the chest up on a single flat colour from the brand palette, with the name in white low on the card. People photographed at different times read as one set because the backdrop, the crop and the name position repeat.
references.apply: One treatment for every featured expert and advisor on the homepage: the same tall crop, a cream or soft teal backdrop where the photo allows, the name in the same place. It also gives the fallback its look: a card with no photo uses the same backdrop with initials, so it belongs to the row. Mental health product.
references.query: therapy service team section with provider portrait cards

references.pattern: 'What do you need help with?' tiles, each with a count of experts
references.why: A serif question heads the section, with two lines that say who the experts are. Each tile has a photo of an expert at work, the need as a serif title, one line on what the help looks like and a count in the link colour ('285 experts'). The count tells the visitor there is someone behind the tile before she clicks.
references.apply: The single need grid for Eleva: six to eight tiles, each with the need in the member's words, one line of example services and a true count ('3 experts'), or 'Opening soon' where there is nobody yet. Use photographs of Eleva's own experts where they agree; a tile with no photo keeps the title, the line and the count. From an email software experts directory; kept for the tile content.
references.query: women's health service categories section with photo tiles

references.pattern: A category grid made only of type and thin rules
references.why: On cream, six cells are divided by thin rules with no boxes, shadows or photographs. Each cell has a two-line serif title, a small count in the accent colour ('16 Biomarkers') and four or five example items that fade out towards the bottom, which says there is more without a link in every cell. The last cell is tinted and holds the one action ('See all tests'). The heading mixes roman and italic serif, close to Eleva's own type.
references.apply: A way to show Eleva's areas of care with no stock photograph: a ruled grid on cream, each cell with the area in Lora, a count of experts and three example services in the member's words, and a last cell that says 'See all experts'. It gives the page one section that is pure typography, which breaks the run of photo cards. Health testing product.
references.query: women's health service categories section with photo tiles

references.pattern: Numbers as rows, each with a sentence and a link to what stands behind it
references.why: Three rows are separated by thin rules. On the left is a very large figure. On the right one plain sentence says what the figure counts, with a text link to where it can be checked ('Browse our templates', 'Read their stories'). Each number leads somewhere, so it reads as a fact and not as decoration.
references.apply: Eleva's 'Who you will meet' block: two or three true figures set large in Lora (experts live, professions, advisors on the board), each with one sentence and a link (See the experts, How we check each expert, Meet the board). A small number set this way looks deliberate. Show only a figure that is true today. From a no-code software product on a dark ground; kept for the row structure.
references.query: health app statistics section with large numbers

references.pattern: Member quotes signed with a first name and the year the member joined
references.why: Each card has a photo across the top, a quote of three to five lines and a signature in two parts: a first name in capitals and 'Calm member since 2017'. The cards are one height, each quote describes a change in the person's own words, and no surname, job title or star rating is shown.
references.apply: The signature for Eleva's member stories: first name, 'Member since 2026' and the area of care. That is enough to be believed and keeps a health story private. Keep quotes to four lines and cards to one height; on a phone show one card with the next one peeking in. Publish only words a member has agreed to share. Meditation product.
references.query: wellness service testimonial section with customer portrait

references.pattern: A large serif headline on off-white over two tiles of unequal width, one a brand pattern
references.why: A two-line serif headline in deep green sits top left with a short paragraph, and the right half of the row stays empty. Below, a narrow tile filled with a brand pattern sits beside a wide photograph of two people talking in a warm room. The pattern tile gives the brand a second image without a second stock photo, and the unequal split keeps the block from looking like a card grid.
references.apply: A composition for Eleva's belief or how-it-works section: a Lora headline at the left, generous empty space, then one photograph at two thirds width beside a teal or cream tile that carries the leaf mark or a simple line pattern. Use it once on the page so it stays distinctive. Software for care practices; kept for the composition.
references.query: health service closing call to action section

references.pattern: Portraits cropped into one brand shape beside a flat colour
references.why: Each statement has one black-and-white portrait cropped into a half circle, with a matching half circle of flat brand colour beside it. The next block mirrors the pair. Photographs of different people look like one series because the crop, the tone and the shape repeat, and the page gets a recognisable image style from very little material.
references.apply: Give Eleva one repeatable treatment for editorial images (for example a soft arch crop with a cream or teal partner shape) in the belief block, the advisor lead and the closing band, in place of rounded rectangles with different light and colour. Keep expert portraits in the directory natural. Mental health company page.
references.query: find a therapist website hero section

references.pattern: FAQ in two columns: the heading and a route to a person on the left, the questions on the right
references.why: The left column holds a two-line heading, one line ('Still got questions? Reach out to our team.') and a small outlined button. The right column holds five questions divided by thin rules, the first one open and a plus sign on the others. The section is short, uses no cards and no background, and the way to reach a person stays in view while reading.
references.apply: The layout for Eleva's homepage FAQ: a Lora heading and 'Still have a question? Write to us' on the left, six questions on the right with ruled lines, the first answer open. On a phone the left column sits above the list. The order of the questions stays as in reference 10. From a payment card product; kept for the layout only.
references.query: FAQ section with a contact support card

references.pattern: A closing line in the visitor's words, a cluster of faces and one action
references.why: On a soft sage ground, one serif sentence speaks to the feeling behind the visit ('You don't have to carry it all alone.'), a short line sits under it, and six round faces overlap in a row. One full-width white row holds the single action. There is no second button and no large image, so the section is calm and takes little height.
references.apply: Eleva's closing action for members, placed after the FAQ and before the expert band: one Lora line in the member's register, a row of small faces of real experts and 'Find an expert' as the one action. The belief statement can live here as that one line. Family care product; the action there is a waiting list.
references.query: final call to action section with photograph for a care service

references.pattern: A line of help with a phone number and an email above the footer links
references.why: Before the link row, the footer says one serif sentence ('Whether it's just a question or to say hello, we're here if you need anything.') and gives two labelled routes, 'Call' and 'General enquiries'. The links themselves are cut to one small row. The last thing on the page is a way to reach a person.
references.apply: Open Eleva's footer with one line and the real help routes (help centre, email), then the Find care column. It answers the missing contact line without adding a column. Show only routes that are answered. From a contacts app on a black ground; kept for the structure.
references.query: final call to action section with photograph for a care service

judging_criteria: Does the hero have one goal (one headline, one line, one action, at most one image or film), and can a first-time visitor choose a need or start a search in the section straight after it? (01-homepage/01 Fresha, 01-homepage/02 Hims)
Does at least one real, bookable expert card (photo or fallback, profession, languages, price from, next slot) appear within the first two screens on a phone? (01-homepage/03 Zocdoc)
Does the expert card still look complete when the expert has no photo and a two-line bio? (01-homepage/04 Glide)
Does the page state that every expert's professional registration is checked, with at least one true number beside it? (01-homepage/05 Hims)
Do the advisors appear once, in a single band with credentials and institutions, placed after the experts and services? (01-homepage/06 Superpower, 01-homepage/07 SwimClub)
Does each 'how it works' step show a piece of the real Eleva interface? (01-homepage/09 Function)
Does the page answer 'what is Eleva, who are the experts, what does it cost' in an FAQ and end with a call to action for members before the expert band? (01-homepage/10 Hims)
On a phone, does the first screen show the headline, its one line and its one action, all easy to read over whatever is behind them? (01-homepage/12 Craft, 01-homepage/14 Biograph)

Do all photographs on the page share one treatment (crop, light, colour or brand shape), with no more than one stock photograph in view at a time? (01-homepage/16 Headspace, 01-homepage/21 Ease, 01-homepage/22 Headspace)

Does each section differ in composition from the one before it (centred, two unequal columns, full-width band, ruled type-only grid), so no two neighbours repeat the same eyebrow, heading and card row? (01-homepage/18 Function, 01-homepage/19 Glide, 01-homepage/21 Ease)
